# subenum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subenum/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#subenum)subenum

Subenum is a simple proc-macro to derive subsets of enums. It allows conversion
between the parent and the child, will derive any traits on the child that you
have on the parent, and will implement `PartialEq` between the parent and child
if you derive it on the parent.

[§](https://docs.rs#simple-example)Simple Example

I think the simplest way to explain it is with an example:

```
use subenum::subenum;
#[subenum(Edible)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Plant {
    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Basil,
    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Tomato,
    Manzanita,
    Pine,
}
fn main() -> Result<(), EdibleConvertError> {
    let plant = Plant::Tomato;
    // We can convert between them.
    let edible = Edible::try_from(plant)?;
    let _plant2 = Plant::from(edible);
    // We can compare them.
    assert_eq!(plant, edible);
    // We derive anything that's derived on the parent, such as clone.
    let edible2 = edible.clone();
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#complex-example)Complex Example

In addition to simple enums and built-in traits, `subenum` works with complex
enums and third-party attributes.

```
use subenum::subenum;
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum AppleType {
    CosmicCrisp,
    Fuji,
    PinkLady,
}
#[subenum(Foo, Tree, Edible, Grass)]
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, strum::Display)]
pub enum Plant<'a, T> {
    #[subenum(Foo)]
    #[strum(serialize = "This is not a plant!")]
    Foo { x: i32, y: i32 },
    #[subenum(Tree, Edible)]
    Apple(AppleType),
    #[subenum(Grass)]
    Bamboo(&'a str),
    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Basil(T),
    #[subenum(Tree)]
    Fir,
    #[subenum(Tree)]
    Pine,
    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Tomato,
    #[subenum(Edible, Grass)]
    Wheat,
}
fn main() -> Result<(), TreeConvertError> {
    let plant: Plant<'_, u32> = Plant::Apple(AppleType::CosmicCrisp);
    let tree = Tree::try_from(plant)?;
    assert_eq!(plant, tree);
    let tree2 = tree.clone();
    assert_eq!(tree2.to_string(), "Apple");
    let foo = Foo::Foo { x: 3, y: 4 };
    assert_eq!(foo.to_string(), "This is not a plant!");
    let edible = Edible::Basil(3);
    let plant = Plant::from(edible);
    assert_eq!(plant.to_string(), "Basil");
    // Can't compare two subenums.
    // assert_ne!(tree2, edible);
    // But we can do some conversion-trickery
    assert_ne!(Plant::from(tree2), Plant::from(edible));
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#subenum-specific-proc-macros)Subenum-specific proc-macros

Maybe you have an enum that can’t be `Copy`d, but the subenum can, and you want
to derive it:

```
use subenum::subenum;
#[subenum(Bar, Qux(derive(Copy)))]
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Clone)]
pub enum Foo {
    #[subenum(Bar)]
    A(String),
    #[subenum(Qux)]
    B,
    #[subenum(Bar, Qux)]
    C(u8),
}
fn main() {
    let b = Qux::B;
    let c = b;
    assert_eq!(b, c);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parent-specific-proc-macros)Parent-specific proc-macros

You can also specify attributes to be added to the parent enums only (i.e., the enum being `subenum`ed) via its same identifier, which can be used for things like documentation:

```
use subenum::subenum;
/// Generic value type
#[subenum(
    Num(doc = "Numeric type\n"), // This will be added to Num itself, but not to Float or Int.
    Float(doc = "Floating point type\n"),
    Int(doc = "Integer type\n")
)]
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Clone, Copy)]
pub enum Num {
    /// 64-bit floating point type (Generic)
    #[subenum(
        Num(doc = "64-bit floating point type (Num)\n"),
        Float(doc = "64-bit floating point type (Float)\n")
    )]
    F64(f64),
    /// 32-bit floating point type (Generic)
    #[subenum(
        Num(doc = "32-bit floating point type (Num)\n"),
        Float(doc = "32-bit floating point type (Float)\n")
    )]
    F32(f32),
    /// 64-bit integer type (Generic)
    #[subenum(
        Num(doc = "64-bit integer type (Num)\n"),
        Int(doc = "64-bit integer type (Int)\n")
    )]
    I64(i64),
    /// 32-bit integer type (Generic)
    #[subenum(
        Num(doc = "32-bit integer type (Num)\n"),
        Int(doc = "32-bit integer type (Int)\n")
    )]
    I32(i32),
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

Bound lifetimes (e.g. `for<'a, 'b, 'c>`) are not currently supported. Please
open a ticket if these are desired.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `default`-- `std`and- `error_trait`
- `std`- Use standard library collections and allocators within this proc macro
- `error_trait`- Implement- `Error`- `ConvertError`types.- When combined with nightly and
`#![feature(error_in_core)]``#[no_std]`
- Otherwise, this feature requires `std`as well.

- When combined with nightly and

([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

## Expand description

    #[subenum(Grass)]

    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Basil(T),
    #[subenum(Tree)]
    Fir,
    #[subenum(Tree)]
    Pine,
    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Tomato,
    #[subenum(Edible, Grass)]
    Wheat,
}
fn main() -> Result<(), TreeConvertError> {
    let plant: Plant<'_, u32> = Plant::Apple(AppleType::CosmicCrisp);
    let tree = Tree::try_from(plant)?;
    assert_eq!(plant, tree);
    let tree2 = tree.clone();
    assert_eq!(tree2.to_string(), "Apple");

    // assert_ne!(tree2, edible);

}
```

# heck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/heck/^0.5.0/

## Expand description

**heck** is a case conversion library.

This library exists to provide case conversion between common cases like CamelCase and snake_case. It is intended to be unicode aware, internally consistent, and reasonably well performing.

[§](https://docs.rs#definition-of-a-word-boundary)Definition of a word boundary

Word boundaries are defined by non-alphanumeric characters, as well as within those words in this manner:

- If an uppercase character is followed by lowercase letters, a word boundary is considered to be just prior to that uppercase character.
- If multiple uppercase characters are consecutive, they are considered to be within a single word, except that the last will be part of the next word if it is followed by lowercase characters (see rule 1).

That is, “HelloWorld” is segmented `Hello|World` whereas “XMLHttpRequest” is
segmented `XML|Http|Request`.

Characters not within words (such as spaces, punctuations, and underscores) are not included in the output string except as they are a part of the case being converted to. Multiple adjacent word boundaries (such as a series of underscores) are folded into one. (“hello__world” in snake case is therefore “hello_world”, not the exact same string). Leading or trailing word boundary indicators are dropped, except insofar as CamelCase capitalizes the first word.

[§](https://docs.rs#cases-contained-in-this-library)Cases contained in this library:

- UpperCamelCase
- lowerCamelCase
- snake_case
- kebab-case
- SHOUTY_SNAKE_CASE
- Title Case
- SHOUTY-KEBAB-CASE
- Train-Case

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AsKebab](https://docs.rs/struct.AsKebabCase.html)- Case
- This wrapper performs a kebab case conversion in `fmt::Display`
- [AsLower](https://docs.rs/struct.AsLowerCamelCase.html)- Camel - Case
- This wrapper performs a lower camel case conversion in `fmt::Display`
- [AsPascal](https://docs.rs/struct.AsPascalCase.html)- Case
- This wrapper performs a upper camel case conversion in `fmt::Display`
- [AsShouty](https://docs.rs/struct.AsShoutyKebabCase.html)- Kebab - Case
- This wrapper performs a kebab case conversion in `fmt::Display`
- [AsShouty](https://docs.rs/struct.AsShoutySnakeCase.html)- Snake - Case
- This wrapper performs a shouty snake  case conversion in `fmt::Display`
- [AsShouty](https://docs.rs/struct.AsShoutySnekCase.html)- Snek - Case
- This wrapper performs a shouty snake  case conversion in `fmt::Display`
- [AsSnake](https://docs.rs/struct.AsSnakeCase.html)- Case
- This wrapper performs a snake case conversion in `fmt::Display`
- [AsSnek](https://docs.rs/struct.AsSnekCase.html)- Case
- This wrapper performs a snake case conversion in `fmt::Display`
- [AsTitle](https://docs.rs/struct.AsTitleCase.html)- Case
- This wrapper performs a title case conversion in `fmt::Display`
- [AsTrain](https://docs.rs/struct.AsTrainCase.html)- Case
- This wrapper performs a train case conversion in `fmt::Display`

# proc_macro2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proc-macro2/^1.0.101/

## Expand description

A wrapper around the procedural macro API of the compiler’s [ proc_macro](https://doc.rust-lang.org/proc_macro/index.html)
crate. This library serves two purposes:

-
**Bring proc-macro-like functionality to other contexts like build.rs and main.rs.**Types from`proc_macro`are entirely specific to procedural macros and cannot ever exist in code outside of a procedural macro. Meanwhile`proc_macro2`types may exist anywhere including non-macro code. By developing foundational libraries like[syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn)and[quote](https://github.com/dtolnay/quote)against`proc_macro2`rather than`proc_macro`, the procedural macro ecosystem becomes easily applicable to many other use cases and we avoid reimplementing non-macro equivalents of those libraries.
-
**Make procedural macros unit testable.**As a consequence of being specific to procedural macros, nothing that uses`proc_macro`can be executed from a unit test. In order for helper libraries or components of a macro to be testable in isolation, they must be implemented using`proc_macro2`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The skeleton of a typical procedural macro typically looks like this:

```
extern crate proc_macro;
#[proc_macro_derive(MyDerive)]
pub fn my_derive(input: proc_macro::TokenStream) -> proc_macro::TokenStream {
    let input = proc_macro2::TokenStream::from(input);
    let output: proc_macro2::TokenStream = {
        /* transform input */
    };
    proc_macro::TokenStream::from(output)
}
```
If parsing with [Syn](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn), you’ll use [ parse_macro_input!](https://docs.rs/syn/2.0/syn/macro.parse_macro_input.html) instead to
propagate parse errors correctly back to the compiler when parsing fails.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

The default feature set of proc-macro2 tracks the most recent stable
compiler API. Functionality in `proc_macro` that is not yet stable is not
exposed by proc-macro2 by default.

To opt into the additional APIs available in the most recent nightly
compiler, the `procmacro2_semver_exempt` config flag must be passed to
rustc. We will polyfill those nightly-only APIs back to Rust 1.68.0. As
these are unstable APIs that track the nightly compiler, minor versions of
proc-macro2 may make breaking changes to them at any time.

`RUSTFLAGS='--cfg procmacro2_semver_exempt' cargo build`Note that this must not only be done for your crate, but for any crate that depends on your crate. This infectious nature is intentional, as it serves as a reminder that you are outside of the normal semver guarantees.

Semver exempt methods are marked as such in the proc-macro2 documentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#thread-safety)Thread-Safety

Most types in this crate are `!Sync` because the underlying compiler
types make use of thread-local memory, meaning they cannot be accessed from
a different thread.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [extra](https://docs.rs/extra/index.html)
- Items which do not have a correspondence to any API in the proc_macro crate, but are necessary to include in proc-macro2.
- [token_](https://docs.rs/token_stream/index.html)- stream
- Public implementation details for the `TokenStream`type, such as iterators.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Group](https://docs.rs/struct.Group.html)
- A delimited token stream.
- [Ident](https://docs.rs/struct.Ident.html)
- A word of Rust code, which may be a keyword or legal variable name.
- [LexError](https://docs.rs/struct.LexError.html)
- Error returned from `TokenStream::from_str`.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineColumn.html)- Column - `span-locations`
- A line-column pair representing the start or end of a `Span`.
- [Literal](https://docs.rs/struct.Literal.html)
- A literal string (`"hello"`), byte string (`b"hello"`), character (`'a'`), byte character (`b'a'`), an integer or floating point number with or without a suffix (`1`,`1u8`,`2.3`,`2.3f32`).
- [Punct](https://docs.rs/struct.Punct.html)
- A `Punct`is a single punctuation character like`+`,`-`or`#`.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A region of source code, along with macro expansion information.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/struct.TokenStream.html)- Stream
- An abstract stream of tokens, or more concretely a sequence of token trees.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Conversion](https://docs.rs/enum.ConversionErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Error when retrieving a string literal’s unescaped value.
- [Delimiter](https://docs.rs/enum.Delimiter.html)
- Describes how a sequence of token trees is delimited.
- [Escape](https://docs.rs/enum.EscapeError.html)- Error - `procmacro2_semver_exempt`
- Errors and warnings that can occur during string, char, and byte unescaping.
- [Spacing](https://docs.rs/enum.Spacing.html)
- Whether a `Punct`is followed immediately by another`Punct`or followed by another token or whitespace.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.TokenTree.html)- Tree
- A single token or a delimited sequence of token trees (e.g. `[1, (), ..]`).

---

# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/^1.0.41/

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.

---

# syn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/syn/^2.0.106/

## Expand description

Syn is a parsing library for parsing a stream of Rust tokens into a syntax tree of Rust source code.

Currently this library is geared toward use in Rust procedural macros, but contains some APIs that may be useful more generally.

-
**Data structures**— Syn provides a complete syntax tree that can represent any valid Rust source code. The syntax tree is rooted at`syn::File``syn::Item``syn::Expr``syn::Type`
-
**Derives**— Of particular interest to derive macros is`syn::DeriveInput`
-
**Parsing**— Parsing in Syn is built around[parser functions](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)with the signature`fn(ParseStream) -> Result<T>`. Every syntax tree node defined by Syn is individually parsable and may be used as a building block for custom syntaxes, or you may dream up your own brand new syntax without involving any of our syntax tree types.
-
**Location information**— Every token parsed by Syn is associated with a`Span`that tracks line and column information back to the source of that token. These spans allow a procedural macro to display detailed error messages pointing to all the right places in the user’s code. There is an example of this below.
-
**Feature flags**— Functionality is aggressively feature gated so your procedural macros enable only what they need, and do not pay in compile time for all the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-of-a-derive-macro)Example of a derive macro

The canonical derive macro using Syn looks like this. We write an ordinary
Rust function tagged with a `proc_macro_derive` attribute and the name of
the trait we are deriving. Any time that derive appears in the user’s code,
the Rust compiler passes their data structure as tokens into our macro. We
get to execute arbitrary Rust code to figure out what to do with those
tokens, then hand some tokens back to the compiler to compile into the
user’s crate.

```
[dependencies]
syn = "2.0"
quote = "1.0"
[lib]
proc-macro = true
```
```
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, DeriveInput};
#[proc_macro_derive(MyMacro)]
pub fn my_macro(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
    // Parse the input tokens into a syntax tree
    let input = parse_macro_input!(input as DeriveInput);
    // Build the output, possibly using quasi-quotation
    let expanded = quote! {
        // ...
    };
    // Hand the output tokens back to the compiler
    TokenStream::from(expanded)
}
```
The [ heapsize](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/heapsize) example directory shows a complete working implementation
of a derive macro. The example derives a

`HeapSize` trait which computes an
estimate of the amount of heap memory owned by a value.```
pub trait HeapSize {
    /// Total number of bytes of heap memory owned by `self`.
    fn heap_size_of_children(&self) -> usize;
}
```
The derive macro allows users to write `#[derive(HeapSize)]` on data
structures in their program.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Demo<'a, T: ?Sized> {
    a: Box<T>,
    b: u8,
    c: &'a str,
    d: String,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#spans-and-error-reporting)Spans and error reporting

The token-based procedural macro API provides great control over where the
compiler’s error messages are displayed in user code. Consider the error the
user sees if one of their field types does not implement `HeapSize`.

```
#[derive(HeapSize)]
struct Broken {
    ok: String,
    bad: std::thread::Thread,
}
```
By tracking span information all the way through the expansion of a
procedural macro as shown in the `heapsize` example, token-based macros in
Syn are able to trigger errors that directly pinpoint the source of the
problem.

```
error[E0277]: the trait bound `std::thread::Thread: HeapSize` is not satisfied
 --> src/main.rs:7:5
  |
7 |     bad: std::thread::Thread,
  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ the trait `HeapSize` is not implemented for `Thread`
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-a-custom-syntax)Parsing a custom syntax

The [ lazy-static](https://github.com/dtolnay/syn/tree/master/examples/lazy-static) example directory shows the implementation of a

`functionlike!(...)` procedural macro in which the input tokens are parsed
using Syn’s parsing API.The example reimplements the popular `lazy_static` crate from crates.io as a
procedural macro.

```
lazy_static! {
    static ref USERNAME: Regex = Regex::new("^[a-z0-9_-]{3,16}$").unwrap();
}
```
The implementation shows how to trigger custom warnings and error messages on the macro input.

```
warning: come on, pick a more creative name
  --> src/main.rs:10:16
   |
10 |     static ref FOO: String = "lazy_static".to_owned();
   |                ^^^
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

When testing macros, we often care not just that the macro can be used
successfully but also that when the macro is provided with invalid input it
produces maximally helpful error messages. Consider using the [ trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
crate to write tests for errors that are emitted by your macro or errors
detected by the Rust compiler in the expanded code following misuse of the
macro. Such tests help avoid regressions from later refactors that
mistakenly make an error no longer trigger or be less helpful than it used
to be.

[§](https://docs.rs#debugging)Debugging

When developing a procedural macro it can be helpful to look at what the
generated code looks like. Use `cargo rustc -- -Zunstable-options -Zunpretty=expanded` or the [ cargo expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) subcommand.

To show the expanded code for some crate that uses your procedural macro,
run `cargo expand` from that crate. To show the expanded code for one of
your own test cases, run `cargo expand --test the_test_case` where the last
argument is the name of the test file without the `.rs` extension.

This write-up by Brandon W Maister discusses debugging in more detail:
[Debugging Rust’s new Custom Derive system](https://quodlibetor.github.io/posts/debugging-rusts-new-custom-derive-system/).

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

Syn puts a lot of functionality behind optional features in order to optimize compile time for the most common use cases. The following features are available.

- `derive`- *(enabled by default)*— Data structures for representing the possible input to a derive macro, including structs and enums and types.
- `full`
- `parsing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to parse input tokens into a syntax tree node of a chosen type.
- `printing`- *(enabled by default)*— Ability to print a syntax tree node as tokens of Rust source code.
- `visit`
- `visit-mut`
- `fold`
- `clone-impls`- *(enabled by default)*— Clone impls for all syntax tree types.
- `extra-traits`
- `proc-macro`- *(enabled by default)*— Runtime dependency on the dynamic library libproc_macro from rustc toolchain.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [buffer](https://docs.rs/buffer/index.html)- `parsing`
- A stably addressed token buffer supporting efficient traversal based on a cheaply copyable cursor.
- [ext](https://docs.rs/ext/index.html)
- Extension traits to provide parsing methods on foreign types.
- [fold](https://docs.rs/fold/index.html)- `fold`
- Syntax tree traversal to transform the nodes of an owned syntax tree.
- [meta](https://docs.rs/meta/index.html)- `parsing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)
- Facility for interpreting structured content inside of an `Attribute`.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/parse/index.html)- `parsing`
- Parsing interface for parsing a token stream into a syntax tree node.
- [punctuated](https://docs.rs/punctuated/index.html)
- A punctuated sequence of syntax tree nodes separated by punctuation.
- [spanned](https://docs.rs/spanned/index.html)- `parsing`and- `printing`
- A trait that can provide the `Span`of the complete contents of a syntax tree node.
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Tokens representing Rust punctuation, keywords, and delimiters.
- [visit](https://docs.rs/visit/index.html)- `visit`
- Syntax tree traversal to walk a shared borrow of a syntax tree.
- [visit_](https://docs.rs/visit_mut/index.html)- mut - `visit-mut`
- Syntax tree traversal to mutate an exclusive borrow of a syntax tree in place.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [Token](https://docs.rs/macro.Token.html)
- A type-macro that expands to the name of the Rust type representation of a given token.
- [braced](https://docs.rs/macro.braced.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of curly braces and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [bracketed](https://docs.rs/macro.bracketed.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of square brackets and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_keyword.html)- keyword
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a given identifier as if it were a keyword.
- [custom_](https://docs.rs/macro.custom_punctuation.html)- punctuation
- Define a type that supports parsing and printing a multi-character symbol as if it were a punctuation token.
- [parenthesized](https://docs.rs/macro.parenthesized.html)- `parsing`
- Parse a set of parentheses and expose their content to subsequent parsers.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_macro_input.html)- macro_ - input - `parsing`and- `proc-macro`
- Parse the input TokenStream of a macro, triggering a compile error if the tokens fail to parse.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote.html)- quote - `parsing`and- `printing`
- Quasi-quotation macro that accepts input like the `quote!`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/macro.parse_quote_spanned.html)- quote_ - spanned - `parsing`and- `printing`
- This macro is `parse_quote!``quote_spanned!`

- A structured list within an attribute, like `derive(Copy, Clone)`.
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/struct.MetaNameValue.html)- Name - Value - `derive`or- `full`
- A name-value pair within an attribute, like `feature = "nightly"`.
- [Parenthesized](https://docs.rs/struct.ParenthesizedGenericArguments.html)- Generic - Arguments - `derive`or- `full`
- Arguments of a function path segment: the `(A, B) -> C`in`Fn(A,B) -> C`.
- [PatConst](https://docs.rs/struct.PatConst.html)- `full`
- A const block: `const { ... }`.
- [PatIdent](https://docs.rs/struct.PatIdent.html)- `full`
- A pattern that binds a new variable: `ref mut binding @ SUBPATTERN`.
- [PatLit](https://docs.rs/struct.PatLit.html)- `full`
- A literal in place of an expression: `1`,`"foo"`.
- [PatMacro](https://docs.rs/struct.PatMacro.html)- `full`
- A macro invocation expression: `format!("{}", q)`.
- [PatOr](https://docs.rs/struct.PatOr.html)- `full`
- A pattern that matches any one of a set of cases.
- [PatParen](https://docs.rs/struct.PatParen.html)- `full`
- A parenthesized pattern: `(A | B)`.
- [PatPath](https://docs.rs/struct.PatPath.html)- `full`
- A path like `core::mem::replace`possibly containing generic parameters and a qualified self-type.
- [PatRange](https://docs.rs/struct.PatRange.html)- `full`
- A range expression: `1..2`,`1..`,`..2`,`1..=2`,`..=2`.
- [PatReference](https://docs.rs/struct.PatReference.html)- `full`
- A reference pattern: `&mut var`.
- [PatRest](https://docs.rs/struct.PatRest.html)- `full`
- The dots in a tuple or slice pattern: `[0, 1, ..]`.
- [PatSlice](https://docs.rs/struct.PatSlice.html)- `full`
- A dynamically sized slice pattern: `[a, b, ref i @ .., y, z]`.
- [PatStruct](https://docs.rs/struct.PatStruct.html)- `full`
- A struct or struct variant pattern: `Variant { x, y, .. }`.
- [PatTuple](https://docs.rs/struct.PatTuple.html)- `full`
- A tuple pattern: `(a, b)`.
- [PatTuple](https://docs.rs/struct.PatTupleStruct.html)- Struct - `full`
- A tuple struct or tuple variant pattern: `Variant(x, y, .., z)`.
- [PatType](https://docs.rs/struct.PatType.html)- `full`
- A type ascription pattern: `foo: f64`.
- [PatWild](https://docs.rs/struct.PatWild.html)- `full`
- A pattern that matches any value: `_`.
- [Path](https://docs.rs/struct.Path.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- A path at which a named item is exported (e.g. `alloc::collections::HashMap`).
- [Path](https://docs.rs/struct.PathSegment.html)- Segment - `derive`or- `full`
- A segment of a path together with any path arguments on that segment.
- [Precise](https://docs.rs/struct.PreciseCapture.html)- Capture - `full`
- Precise capturing bound: the ‘use<…>’ in `impl Trait + use<'a, T>`.
- [Predicate](https://docs.rs/struct.PredicateLifetime.html)- Lifetime - `derive`or- `full`
- A lifetime predicate in a `where`clause:`'a: 'b + 'c`.
- [Predicate](https://docs.rs/struct.PredicateType.html)- Type - `derive`or- `full`
- A type predicate in a `where`clause:`for<'c> Foo<'c>: Trait<'c>`.
- [QSelf](https://docs.rs/struct.QSelf.html)- `derive`or- `full`
- The explicit Self type in a qualified path: the `T`in`<T as Display>::fmt`.
- [Receiver](https://docs.rs/struct.Receiver.html)- `full`
- The `self`argument of an associated method.
- [Signature](https://docs.rs/struct.Signature.html)- `full`
- A function signature in a trait or implementation: `unsafe fn initialize(&self)`.
- [Stmt](https://docs.rs/struct.StmtMacro.html)- Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation in statement position.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitBound.html)- Bound - `derive`or- `full`
- A trait used as a bound on a type parameter.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemConst.html)- Item - Const - `full`
- An associated constant within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemFn.html)- Item - Fn - `full`
- An associated function within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemMacro.html)- Item - Macro - `full`
- A macro invocation within the definition of a trait.
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/struct.TraitItemType.html)- Item - Type - `full`
- An associated type within the definition of a trait.
- [Turbofish](https://docs.rs/struct.Turbofish.html)- `printing`and (- `derive`or- `full`)

- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeParam.html)- Param - `derive`or- `full`
- A generic type parameter: `T: Into<String>`.

- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypePath.html)- Path - `derive`or- `full`

# derive_more - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/derive_more/^2.1.1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#derive_more)`derive_more`

Rust has lots of builtin traits that are implemented for its basic types, such
as `Add`, `Not`, `From` or `Display`.
However, when wrapping these types inside your own structs or enums you lose the
implementations of these traits and are required to recreate them.
This is especially annoying when your own structures are very simple, such as
when using the commonly advised newtype pattern (e.g. `MyInt(i32)`).

This library tries to remove these annoyances and the corresponding boilerplate code. It does this by allowing you to derive lots of commonly used traits for both structs and enums.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-code)Example code

By using this library the following code just works:

```
use derive_more::{Add, Display, From, Into};
#[derive(PartialEq, From, Add)]
struct MyInt(i32);
#[derive(PartialEq, From, Into)]
struct Point2D {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}
#[derive(PartialEq, From, Add, Display)]
enum MyEnum {
    #[display("int: {_0}")]
    Int(i32),
    Uint(u32),
    #[display("nothing")]
    Nothing,
}
assert!(MyInt(11) == MyInt(5) + 6.into());
assert!((5, 6) == Point2D { x: 5, y: 6 }.into());
assert!(MyEnum::Int(15) == (MyEnum::Int(8) + 7.into()).unwrap());
assert!(MyEnum::Int(15).to_string() == "int: 15");
assert!(MyEnum::Uint(42).to_string() == "42");
assert!(MyEnum::Nothing.to_string() == "nothing");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-derivable-traits)The derivable traits

Below are all the traits that you can derive using this library. Some trait derivations are so similar that the further documentation will only show a single one of them. You can recognize these by the “-like” suffix in their name. The trait name before that will be the only one that is used throughout the further documentation.

It is important to understand what code gets generated when using one of the derives from this crate. That is why the links below explain what code gets generated for a trait for each group from before.

You can use the [ cargo-expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) utility to see the exact code that is generated
for your specific type.
This will show you your code with all macros and derives expanded.

**NOTE**: You still have to derive each trait separately. So `#[derive(Mul)]` doesn’t
automatically derive `Div` as well. To derive both you should do `#[derive(Mul, Div)]`

[§](https://docs.rs#conversion-traits)Conversion traits

These are traits that are used to convert automatically between types.

[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-traits)Formatting traits

These traits are used for converting a struct to a string in different ways.

- `Debug`
- `Display`-like- `Display`,- `Binary`,- `Octal`,- `LowerHex`,- `UpperHex`,- `LowerExp`,- `UpperExp`,- `Pointer`

[§](https://docs.rs#error-handling-traits)Error-handling traits

These traits are used to define error-types.

[§](https://docs.rs#operators)Operators

These are traits that can be used for operator overloading.

- `Index`
- `Deref`
- `Not`-like- `Not`and- `Neg`
- `Add`-like- `Add`,- `Sub`,- `BitAnd`,- `BitOr`,- `BitXor`
- `Mul`-like- `Mul`,- `Div`,- `Rem`,- `Shr`and- `Shl`
- `Sum`-like- `Sum`and- `Product`
- `IndexMut`
- `DerefMut`
- `AddAssign`-like- `AddAssign`,- `SubAssign`,- `BitAndAssign`,- `BitOrAssign`and- `BitXorAssign`
- `MulAssign`-like- `MulAssign`,- `DivAssign`,- `RemAssign`,- `ShrAssign`and- `ShlAssign`
- `Eq`- `PartialEq`

[§](https://docs.rs#static-methods)Static methods

These don’t derive traits, but derive static methods instead.

- `Constructor`- `new`method that can be used as a constructor. This is very basic if you need more customization for your constructor, check out the- `derive-new`
- `IsVariant`- `foo`of an enum type, derives a- `is_foo`method.
- `Unwrap`- `foo`of an enum type, derives an- `unwrap_foo`method.
- `TryUnwrap`- `foo`of an enum type, derives an- `try_unwrap_foo`method.

[§](https://docs.rs#re-exports)Re-exports

This crate also re-exports all the standard library traits, that it adds derives
for, in the `with_trait` module. So, both the `Display` derive and the `Display`
trait will be in scope when you add the following code:

`use derive_more::with_trait::Display; // also imports `core::fmt::Display``By default, derive macros only, without the corresponding traits, are imported from
the crate’s root (or from the `derive` module):

```
use derive_more::Display;   // imports macro only
use derive_more::derive::*; // imports all macros only
```
[§](https://docs.rs#hygiene)Hygiene

For hygiene purposes, macros use `derive_more::*` absolute paths in their expansions.
This might introduce a trouble, if you want to re-export `derive_more` macros in your
own crate without using the `derive_more` as a direct dependency in downstream crates:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use my_lib::Display; // re-exported in `my_lib` crate
#[derive(Display)] // error: could not find `derive_more` in the list of imported crates
struct MyInt(i32);
```
In such case, you should re-export the `derive_more` module too:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use my_lib::{derive_more, Display}; // re-exported in `my_lib` crate
#[derive(Display)] // works fine now!
struct MyInt(i32);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#installation)Installation

To avoid redundant compilation times, by default no derives are supported.
You have to enable each type of derive as a feature in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
# You can specify the types of derives that you need for less time spent
# compiling. For the full list of features see this crate its `Cargo.toml`.
derive_more = { version = "2", features = ["from", "add", "into_iterator"] }
```
```
[dependencies]
# If you don't care much about compilation times and simply want to have
# support for all the possible derives, you can use the "full" feature.
derive_more = { version = "2", features = ["full"] }
```
```
[dependencies]
# If you run in a `no_std` environment you should disable the default features,
# because the only default feature is the "std" feature.
# NOTE: You can combine this with "full" feature to get support for all the
#       possible derives in a `no_std` environment.
derive_more = { version = "2", default-features = false }
```
And this to the top of your Rust file:

```
// use the derives that you want in the file
use derive_more::{Add, Display, From};
```
If you’re still using Rust 2015, add this instead:

This library requires Rust 1.81 or higher.

Changing [MSRV](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-rust-version-field) (minimum supported Rust version) of this crate is treated as a **minor version change** in terms of [Semantic Versioning](http://semver.org).

- So, if [MSRV](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-rust-version-field)changes are**NOT concerning**for your project, just use the default[caret requirement](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/specifying-dependencies.html#caret-requirements):`[dependencies] derive_more = "2" # or "2.1", or "^2.1"`
- However, if [MSRV](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-rust-version-field)changes are concerning for your project, then use the[tilde requirement](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/specifying-dependencies.html#tilde-requirements)to**pin to a specific minor version**:`[dependencies] derive_more = "~2.1" # or "~2.1.1"`

# strum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/strum/^0.28.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#strum)Strum

Strum is a set of macros and traits for working with enums and strings easier in Rust.

The full version of the README can be found on [GitHub](https://github.com/Peternator7/strum).

[§](https://docs.rs#including-strum-in-your-project)Including Strum in Your Project

Import strum and `strum_macros` into your project by adding the following lines to your
Cargo.toml. `strum_macros` contains the macros needed to derive all the traits in Strum.

```
[dependencies]
strum = "0.28"
strum_macros = "0.28"
# You can also access strum_macros exports directly through strum using the "derive" feature
strum = { version = "0.28", features = ["derive"] }
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [additional_](https://docs.rs/additional_attributes/index.html)- attributes
- Documentation for Additional Attributes

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Parse](https://docs.rs/enum.ParseError.html)- Error
- The `ParseError`enum is a collection of all the possible reasons an enum can fail to parse from a string.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AsStatic](https://docs.rs/trait.AsStaticRef.html)- Ref - Deprecated
- A cheap reference-to-reference conversion. Used to convert a value to a
reference value with `'static`lifetime within generic code.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/trait.EnumCount.html)- Count
- A trait for capturing the number of variants in Enum. This trait can be autoderived by
`strum_macros`.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/trait.EnumMessage.html)- Message
- Associates additional pieces of information with an Enum. This can be
autoimplemented by deriving `EnumMessage`and annotating your variants with`#[strum(message="...")]`.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/trait.EnumProperty.html)- Property
- `EnumProperty`is a trait that makes it possible to store additional information with enum variants. This trait is designed to be used with the macro of the same name in the- `strum_macros`crate. Currently, the string, integer and bool literals are supported in attributes.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoDiscriminant.html)- Discriminant
- A trait for retrieving the enum generated by `EnumDiscriminants``strum_macros`.
- [Into](https://docs.rs/trait.IntoEnumIterator.html)- Enum - Iterator
- This trait designates that an `Enum`can be iterated over. It can be auto generated using the`EnumIter`
- [Variant](https://docs.rs/trait.VariantArray.html)- Array
- A trait for retrieving a static array containing all the variants in an Enum.
This trait can be autoderived by `strum_macros`. For derived usage, all the variants in the enumerator need to be unit-types, which means you can’t autoderive enums with inner data in one or more variants. Consider using it alongside`EnumDiscriminants`
- [Variant](https://docs.rs/trait.VariantIterator.html)- Iterator
- [Variant](https://docs.rs/trait.VariantMetadata.html)- Metadata
- [Variant](https://docs.rs/trait.VariantNames.html)- Names
- A trait for retrieving the names of each variant in Enum. This trait can
be autoderived by `strum_macros`.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [AsRef](https://docs.rs/derive.AsRefStr.html)- Str - `derive`
- Converts enum variants to `&'a str`, where`'a`is the lifetime of the input enum reference.
- [Display](https://docs.rs/derive.Display.html)- `derive`
- Converts enum variants to strings.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/derive.EnumCount.html)- Count - `derive`
- Add a constant `usize`equal to the number of variants.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/derive.EnumDiscriminants.html)- Discriminants - `derive`
- Generate a new type with only the discriminant names.
- [EnumIs](https://docs.rs/derive.EnumIs.html)- `derive`
- Generated `is_*()`methods for each variant. E.g.`Color.is_red()`.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/derive.EnumIter.html)- Iter - `derive`
- Creates a new type that iterates over the variants of an enum.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/derive.EnumMessage.html)- Message - `derive`
- Add a verbose message to an enum variant.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/derive.EnumProperty.html)- Property - `derive`
- Add custom properties to enum variants.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/derive.EnumString.html)- String - `derive`
- Converts strings to enum variants based on their name.
- [Enum](https://docs.rs/derive.EnumTryAs.html)- TryAs - `derive`
- Generated `try_as_*()`methods for all tuple-style variants. E.g.`Message.try_as_write()`.
- [From](https://docs.rs/derive.FromRepr.html)- Repr - `derive`
- Add a function to enum that allows accessing variants by its discriminant
- [Into](https://docs.rs/derive.IntoStaticStr.html)- Static - Str - `derive`
- Implements `From<MyEnum> for &'static str`on an enum.
- [Variant](https://docs.rs/derive.VariantArray.html)- Array - `derive`
- Adds a `'static`slice with all of the Enum’s variants.
- [Variant](https://docs.rs/derive.VariantNames.html)- Names - `derive`
- Implements `Strum::VariantNames`which adds an associated constant`VARIANTS`which is a`'static`slice of discriminant names.

# subenum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/subenum/latest/target-redirect/subenum/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#subenum)subenum

Subenum is a simple proc-macro to derive subsets of enums. It allows conversion
between the parent and the child, will derive any traits on the child that you
have on the parent, and will implement `PartialEq` between the parent and child
if you derive it on the parent.

[§](https://docs.rs#simple-example)Simple Example

I think the simplest way to explain it is with an example:

```
use subenum::subenum;
#[subenum(Edible)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Plant {
    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Basil,
    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Tomato,
    Manzanita,
    Pine,
}
fn main() -> Result<(), EdibleConvertError> {
    let plant = Plant::Tomato;
    // We can convert between them.
    let edible = Edible::try_from(plant)?;
    let _plant2 = Plant::from(edible);
    // We can compare them.
    assert_eq!(plant, edible);
    // We derive anything that's derived on the parent, such as clone.
    let edible2 = edible.clone();
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#complex-example)Complex Example

In addition to simple enums and built-in traits, `subenum` works with complex
enums and third-party attributes.

```
use subenum::subenum;
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum AppleType {
    CosmicCrisp,
    Fuji,
    PinkLady,
}
#[subenum(Foo, Tree, Edible, Grass)]
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, strum::Display)]
pub enum Plant<'a, T> {
    #[subenum(Foo)]
    #[strum(serialize = "This is not a plant!")]
    Foo { x: i32, y: i32 },
    #[subenum(Tree, Edible)]
    Apple(AppleType),
    #[subenum(Grass)]
    Bamboo(&'a str),
    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Basil(T),
    #[subenum(Tree)]
    Fir,
    #[subenum(Tree)]
    Pine,
    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Tomato,
    #[subenum(Edible, Grass)]
    Wheat,
}
fn main() -> Result<(), TreeConvertError> {
    let plant: Plant<'_, u32> = Plant::Apple(AppleType::CosmicCrisp);
    let tree = Tree::try_from(plant)?;
    assert_eq!(plant, tree);
    let tree2 = tree.clone();
    assert_eq!(tree2.to_string(), "Apple");
    let foo = Foo::Foo { x: 3, y: 4 };
    assert_eq!(foo.to_string(), "This is not a plant!");
    let edible = Edible::Basil(3);
    let plant = Plant::from(edible);
    assert_eq!(plant.to_string(), "Basil");
    // Can't compare two subenums.
    // assert_ne!(tree2, edible);
    // But we can do some conversion-trickery
    assert_ne!(Plant::from(tree2), Plant::from(edible));
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#subenum-specific-proc-macros)Subenum-specific proc-macros

Maybe you have an enum that can’t be `Copy`d, but the subenum can, and you want
to derive it:

```
use subenum::subenum;
#[subenum(Bar, Qux(derive(Copy)))]
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Clone)]
pub enum Foo {
    #[subenum(Bar)]
    A(String),
    #[subenum(Qux)]
    B,
    #[subenum(Bar, Qux)]
    C(u8),
}
fn main() {
    let b = Qux::B;
    let c = b;
    assert_eq!(b, c);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parent-specific-proc-macros)Parent-specific proc-macros

You can also specify attributes to be added to the parent enums only (i.e., the enum being `subenum`ed) via its same identifier, which can be used for things like documentation:

```
use subenum::subenum;
/// Generic value type
#[subenum(
    Num(doc = "Numeric type\n"), // This will be added to Num itself, but not to Float or Int.
    Float(doc = "Floating point type\n"),
    Int(doc = "Integer type\n")
)]
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Clone, Copy)]
pub enum Num {
    /// 64-bit floating point type (Generic)
    #[subenum(
        Num(doc = "64-bit floating point type (Num)\n"),
        Float(doc = "64-bit floating point type (Float)\n")
    )]
    F64(f64),
    /// 32-bit floating point type (Generic)
    #[subenum(
        Num(doc = "32-bit floating point type (Num)\n"),
        Float(doc = "32-bit floating point type (Float)\n")
    )]
    F32(f32),
    /// 64-bit integer type (Generic)
    #[subenum(
        Num(doc = "64-bit integer type (Num)\n"),
        Int(doc = "64-bit integer type (Int)\n")
    )]
    I64(i64),
    /// 32-bit integer type (Generic)
    #[subenum(
        Num(doc = "32-bit integer type (Num)\n"),
        Int(doc = "32-bit integer type (Int)\n")
    )]
    I32(i32),
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

Bound lifetimes (e.g. `for<'a, 'b, 'c>`) are not currently supported. Please
open a ticket if these are desired.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `default`-- `std`and- `error_trait`
- `std`- Use standard library collections and allocators within this proc macro
- `error_trait`- Implement- `Error`- `ConvertError`types.- When combined with nightly and
`#![feature(error_in_core)]``#[no_std]`
- Otherwise, this feature requires `std`as well.

- When combined with nightly and

- MIT license
([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# subenum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/subenum

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#subenum)subenum

Subenum is a simple proc-macro to derive subsets of enums. It allows conversion
between the parent and the child, will derive any traits on the child that you
have on the parent, and will implement `PartialEq` between the parent and child
if you derive it on the parent.

[§](https://docs.rs#simple-example)Simple Example

I think the simplest way to explain it is with an example:

```
use subenum::subenum;
#[subenum(Edible)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Plant {
    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Basil,
    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Tomato,
    Manzanita,
    Pine,
}
fn main() -> Result<(), EdibleConvertError> {
    let plant = Plant::Tomato;
    // We can convert between them.
    let edible = Edible::try_from(plant)?;
    let _plant2 = Plant::from(edible);
    // We can compare them.
    assert_eq!(plant, edible);
    // We derive anything that's derived on the parent, such as clone.
    let edible2 = edible.clone();
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#complex-example)Complex Example

In addition to simple enums and built-in traits, `subenum` works with complex
enums and third-party attributes.

```
use subenum::subenum;
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum AppleType {
    CosmicCrisp,
    Fuji,
    PinkLady,
}
#[subenum(Foo, Tree, Edible, Grass)]
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, strum::Display)]
pub enum Plant<'a, T> {
    #[subenum(Foo)]
    #[strum(serialize = "This is not a plant!")]
    Foo { x: i32, y: i32 },
    #[subenum(Tree, Edible)]
    Apple(AppleType),
    #[subenum(Grass)]
    Bamboo(&'a str),
    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Basil(T),
    #[subenum(Tree)]
    Fir,
    #[subenum(Tree)]
    Pine,
    #[subenum(Edible)]
    Tomato,
    #[subenum(Edible, Grass)]
    Wheat,
}
fn main() -> Result<(), TreeConvertError> {
    let plant: Plant<'_, u32> = Plant::Apple(AppleType::CosmicCrisp);
    let tree = Tree::try_from(plant)?;
    assert_eq!(plant, tree);
    let tree2 = tree.clone();
    assert_eq!(tree2.to_string(), "Apple");
    let foo = Foo::Foo { x: 3, y: 4 };
    assert_eq!(foo.to_string(), "This is not a plant!");
    let edible = Edible::Basil(3);
    let plant = Plant::from(edible);
    assert_eq!(plant.to_string(), "Basil");
    // Can't compare two subenums.
    // assert_ne!(tree2, edible);
    // But we can do some conversion-trickery
    assert_ne!(Plant::from(tree2), Plant::from(edible));
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#subenum-specific-proc-macros)Subenum-specific proc-macros

Maybe you have an enum that can’t be `Copy`d, but the subenum can, and you want
to derive it:

```
use subenum::subenum;
#[subenum(Bar, Qux(derive(Copy)))]
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Clone)]
pub enum Foo {
    #[subenum(Bar)]
    A(String),
    #[subenum(Qux)]
    B,
    #[subenum(Bar, Qux)]
    C(u8),
}
fn main() {
    let b = Qux::B;
    let c = b;
    assert_eq!(b, c);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#parent-specific-proc-macros)Parent-specific proc-macros

You can also specify attributes to be added to the parent enums only (i.e., the enum being `subenum`ed) via its same identifier, which can be used for things like documentation:

```
use subenum::subenum;
/// Generic value type
#[subenum(
    Num(doc = "Numeric type\n"), // This will be added to Num itself, but not to Float or Int.
    Float(doc = "Floating point type\n"),
    Int(doc = "Integer type\n")
)]
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Clone, Copy)]
pub enum Num {
    /// 64-bit floating point type (Generic)
    #[subenum(
        Num(doc = "64-bit floating point type (Num)\n"),
        Float(doc = "64-bit floating point type (Float)\n")
    )]
    F64(f64),
    /// 32-bit floating point type (Generic)
    #[subenum(
        Num(doc = "32-bit floating point type (Num)\n"),
        Float(doc = "32-bit floating point type (Float)\n")
    )]
    F32(f32),
    /// 64-bit integer type (Generic)
    #[subenum(
        Num(doc = "64-bit integer type (Num)\n"),
        Int(doc = "64-bit integer type (Int)\n")
    )]
    I64(i64),
    /// 32-bit integer type (Generic)
    #[subenum(
        Num(doc = "32-bit integer type (Num)\n"),
        Int(doc = "32-bit integer type (Int)\n")
    )]
    I32(i32),
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

Bound lifetimes (e.g. `for<'a, 'b, 'c>`) are not currently supported. Please
open a ticket if these are desired.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `default`-- `std`and- `error_trait`
- `std`- Use standard library collections and allocators within this proc macro
- `error_trait`- Implement- `Error`- `ConvertError`types.- When combined with nightly and
`#![feature(error_in_core)]``#[no_std]`
- Otherwise, this feature requires `std`as well.

- When combined with nightly and

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0 ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license
([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

# pivx_rpc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pivx-rpc/0.4.0/pivx_rpc/

## Expand description

PIVX SDK: typed JSON-RPC client for pivxd with first-class support for shielded (SHIELD/Sapling) balances and transactions.

```
use pivx_rpc::{Auth, PivxClient, ShieldRecipient, ShieldWatcher, WatchOptions};
let client = PivxClient::new(
    "http://127.0.0.1:51473",
    Auth::UserPass { user: "rpcuser".into(), pass: "rpcpass".into() },
)?;
// Watch a shielded address via its viewing key (no spend key needed).
let imported = client.import_sapling_viewing_key("p-view-key...", None, None).await?;
let mut watcher = ShieldWatcher::new(&client, WatchOptions {
    addresses: vec![imported.address],
    ..Default::default()
});
let events = watcher.poll().await?; // first poll primes silently
// Send shielded funds (node wallet holds the keys and builds the proof).
let txid = client
    .shield_send_many(
        pivx_rpc::FromAddress::AnyShield,
        &[ShieldRecipient::new("ps1...", 1.5).with_memo("hello")],
    )
    .await?;
```

# sim_lib_pitch_namer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-pitch-namer/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_pitch_namer/

## Expand description

Multi-school cluster naming for the SIM music libraries.

This crate is the aggregator over the pitch-naming schools. It defines the
shared [ ClusterNamer](https://docs.rs/trait.ClusterNamer.html) trait and the

[taxonomy, then drives every built-in school – Forte set-class names, functional roman numerals, plain set-theory prime forms, neo-Riemannian labels, and jazz chord symbols – through one](https://docs.rs/enum.NamingSchool.html)

`NamingSchool`[. The registry can label a pitch-class set in every school at once and translate a label from one school to another. The schools themselves live in the](https://docs.rs/struct.NamerRegistry.html)

`NamerRegistry``sim-lib-pitch-namer-*` sibling crates; this
crate composes them and exposes them as a SIM runtime library through
[/](https://docs.rs/struct.PitchNamerLib.html)

`PitchNamerLib`[.](https://docs.rs/fn.install_pitch_namer_lib.html)

`install_pitch_namer_lib`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Cluster](https://docs.rs/struct.ClusterLabel.html)- Label
- A label produced by one naming school for one pitch-class set.
- [Cluster](https://docs.rs/struct.ClusterMeta.html)- Meta
- Metadata attached to a produced `ClusterLabel`
- [Label](https://docs.rs/struct.LabelContext.html)- Context
- The context a namer may use: an optional chord root and an optional key.
- [Namer](https://docs.rs/struct.NamerRegistry.html)- Registry
- A registry of `ClusterNamer`
- [Pitch](https://docs.rs/struct.PitchNamerLib.html)- Namer - Lib
- Host-registered lib exporting the built-in cluster-namer cards and registry,
built on the shared `SurfacePackLib`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Naming](https://docs.rs/enum.NamingSchool.html)- School
- A school of chord and pitch-set naming.
- [Pitch](https://docs.rs/enum.PitchNamerError.html)- Namer - Error
- Error returned by naming-registry operations.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Cluster](https://docs.rs/trait.ClusterNamer.html)- Namer
- A namer that labels a pitch-class set within one `NamingSchool`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [install_](https://docs.rs/fn.install_pitch_namer_lib.html)- pitch_ - namer_ - lib
- Installs the `PitchNamerLib``cx`, registering each namer’s export record; installing more than once is a no-op.

# facett - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett/0.1.10/facett/

## Expand description

**facett** — umbrella crate. One dependency that re-exports every component,
so a consumer writes `facett::graph::GraphView` / `facett::map::MapView` etc.
instead of pulling each `facett-*` crate. The `Facet` model + the headless
test `harness` are at the root.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [clip](https://docs.rs/clip/index.html)
- **Cross-facet typed copy/paste**(§16) — the trait + payload machinery so copy/paste carries- **full typed data**between facett components, not just text. A process-wide transfer registry holds the last typed- `ClipPayload`
- [effects](https://docs.rs/effects/index.html)
- **effects**— motion + bloom for the facett look. Pure egui,- **glow backend only**: everything here paints with layered alpha shapes on an- `egui::Painter`
- [harness](https://docs.rs/harness/index.html)
- Headless test harness — **fire up a**: its`Facet`, inject data, render it offscreen, and capture what it drew`state_json`+ a vertex count (a “it drew something” proxy) + a stderr activity trail. No display, no GPU. This is the basis of facett’s auto test matrix, and mirrors nornir viz’s`NORNIR_VIZ_STATE`introspection — every component is observable from outside.
- [look](https://docs.rs/look/index.html)
- **facett look & feel**(the work-order architecture, §3) — one- `Theme`- **Windows**,- **macOS**,- **Device**(effects-off, rugged/military). The- `Theme`- *single source of truth*:- `Theme::apply`- `egui::Style`(visuals + spacing + scroll) plus the text scale in one call, and also publishes the derived legacy- `crate::Theme`
- [nav](https://docs.rs/nav/index.html)
- **Shared spatial navigation + focus**(§13 FOC-2, §14 NAV-1) — the- *one*pan/zoom model (- `Navigable`) reused by map/graph/plot/canvas, and the- *one*spatial focus rule (- `nearest_in_direction`) reused by pane and form navigation (COH-3). Pan/zoom is expressed as an- `egui::emath::TSTransform`(scale + offset), so a host can also use it to transform an overlaid guest layer (§5 CMP-4).
- [scroll_](https://docs.rs/scroll_engine/index.html)- engine
- **CygnusEd smooth-scroll engine**(§11) — pixel-by-pixel, sub-pixel soft scrolling with momentum/acceleration, à la the Amiga editor’s jerkyless feel. The scroll- *offset*is decoupled from row height (renderers paint at a- **fractional**pixel offset + clip), and the whole thing is- **deterministic under an injected clock**(- `advance(dt)`), so snapshots reproduce exactly (FC-7 / P0-5). Reusable by text, console, and the dataframe grid (SCRL-3).
- [theme](https://docs.rs/theme/index.html)
- **Theming.**A palette the custom-painted components (graph/depgraph/map) read from the egui context, plus matching egui- `Visuals`for the standard widgets (pop/table/pipeline). Call- `set_theme`- `Theme::default`- `Theme::sci_fi`- `Theme::nordic_aurora`- `Theme::cyberpunk_neon`- `Theme::amber_crt`- `Theme::deep_space`- `Theme::hugin_noir`- `Theme::ALL`- `Theme::by_name`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arrow](https://docs.rs/struct.ArrowColumnRef.html)- Column - Ref
- One named Arrow column, shared zero-copy. The `Arc<dyn Array>`is the same buffer the source holds — copying a grid column never clones the data.
- [Edge](https://docs.rs/struct.Edge.html)
- A directed edge between node indices.
- [Facet](https://docs.rs/struct.FacetDeck.html)- Deck
- A tabbed set of `Facet`**every**facet’s`state_json`under its title, so the whole-app introspection contract is free. korp/nornir can build their window from a`FacetDeck`instead of hand-rolling tabs + the state dump.
- [KeyMap](https://docs.rs/struct.KeyMap.html)
- `Action → KeyboardShortcut`. Serialisable (KeyboardShortcut is serde in egui), so a host can save/load a remapped keymap (KEY-6). Uses- `Modifiers::COMMAND`which egui maps to ⌘ on macOS / Ctrl elsewhere (KEY-3).
- [Look](https://docs.rs/struct.LookTheme.html)- Theme
- The one theme (ARCH-1). Every sub-struct is fully populated by every preset
(no leaked defaults, ARCH-3); fields are public with `with_*`builders (ARCH-5); the whole thing is`serde`(ARCH-4).
- [Navigable](https://docs.rs/struct.Navigable.html)
- The shared pan/zoom model (NAV-1). Stores a scale + translation as a
`TSTransform`mapping**scene → screen**. Map, graph and plot all drive this with the same gestures, so they feel identical (NAV-2).
- [Node](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html)
- A node: a label + a colour (the *consumer*picks the colour policy — hash by label, by status, …).
- [Scene](https://docs.rs/struct.Scene.html)
- A drawable graph: nodes + edges (edges index into `nodes`).
- [Smooth](https://docs.rs/struct.SmoothScroll.html)- Scroll
- A 1-D smooth scroll axis. `offset`is the current (fractional) pixel offset;`target`is where we’re easing toward;`velocity`carries momentum after a flick. Advance with`advance`
- [Theme](https://docs.rs/struct.Theme.html)
- The facett palette. All custom-painted colours come from here.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Action](https://docs.rs/enum.Action.html)
- The single semantic action vocabulary shared by every facett component
(COH-2). A given action is the **same chord in every component**because the chord lives only here, in the`KeyMap`
- [Clip](https://docs.rs/enum.ClipKind.html)- Kind
- The kinds a payload can take. `Custom`is the extension point.
- [Clip](https://docs.rs/enum.ClipPayload.html)- Payload
- A typed clipboard payload. The richest form a source can offer; a target picks
the best representation it accepts (negotiation in [`PasteTarget::paste`]).
- [Dir4](https://docs.rs/enum.Dir4.html)
- A compass direction for directional focus / pane moves.
- [Layout](https://docs.rs/enum.Layout.html)
- Node placement strategy.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Copy](https://docs.rs/trait.CopySource.html)- Source
- A component that can **produce**a typed payload from its current selection.
- [Facet](https://docs.rs/trait.Facet.html)
- The facett **component contract**. Every facet — graph, map, pipeline, table, the ported nornir viewers — implements this, so consumers (korp, nornir, …) compose them uniformly*and*get headless robot-testing for free.
- [Paste](https://docs.rs/trait.PasteTarget.html)- Target
- A component that can **accept**a pasted payload.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [draw](https://docs.rs/fn.draw.html)
- Draw a `Scene`into`ui`— the reusable render primitive. Empty scenes show`empty_hint`. Labels render when the node count is small enough to read.
- [hash_](https://docs.rs/fn.hash_color.html)- color
- A stable, bright-ish colour from a string (FNV-1a). Handy default node colour.
- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_theme.html)- theme
- Store `theme`on the context**and**apply its egui`Visuals`. Call once per frame (cheap) or whenever the theme changes; every facet picks it up.
- [theme](https://docs.rs/fn.theme.html)
- The theme stored on the ui’s context (or `Theme::default`

# facett_map3d_flight - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-map3d-flight/0.1.10/facett_map3d_flight/

## Expand description

**facett-map3d-flight** — the AAA planetary **FLIGHT-SIM** engine layer over the
lightweight, embeddable [ facett_map3d](https://docs.rs/facett-map3d/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_map3d/index.html) map. This crate carries the heavy,
GPU-required, full-screen “bells and whistles”;

`facett-map3d` stays lean
(flat ground + extruded house markers, CPU-fallback, deck-pane-embeddable).[§](https://docs.rs#what-has-landed-here-cpu-foundation--build--test-green-headless)What has LANDED here (CPU foundation — build + test green, headless)

- `origin`- **floating origin**: an- `f64`Web-Mercator world frame + per-frame camera-centred rebase to- `f32`, killing far-from-origin vertex jitter / Z-fighting at planetary scale (FLIGHT-SIM #1).
- `atmos`- **precomputed atmospheric scattering**: a Bruneton/Hillaire-style transmittance LUT + single-scatter sky-view + aerial perspective, feeding both the sky AND the terrain/building haze, varying with altitude + sun angle (FLIGHT-SIM #2). Derived sky tints are ready to drive- `facett_map3d`’s existing analytic- `sky.wgsl`uniforms.
- `camera_fly`- **camera rig**: a deterministic 6DOF state machine (free-fly primary / cinematic orbit / flight-stick) over the- `f64`world frame, exercising the floating origin.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-roadmapped--spiked-see-nornirflightsim-engine-roadmapmd)What is ROADMAPPED / spiked (see `.nornir/flightsim-engine-roadmap.md`)

GPU scattering-LUT precompute pass, GPU-compute building extrusion (BuildingMeta
marshaller + indirect draw), CDLOD/quadtree DEM terrain + the drape fix, and the
out-of-core Hilbert-sorted GeoParquet streaming. The shared `Mesh3` + wgpu
pipeline + sky/water shaders are **reused** from `facett_map3d` (re-exported
below), not forked.

Everything that lands here is pure CPU math (no GPU, no egui at the foundation layer), so the precision + scattering + rig invariants are directly inject-assert-testable and deterministic (FC-7).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)
